If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students can tell the difference between dignity (worth everyone has) and respect (earned), and between belonging and fitting in; recognize small moments that build or break belonging; and choose one way to widen the circle this week. Nobody is asked to share a time they were left out or excluded someone.

Materials

  • The deck on the big screen. Each slide carries its own point, so no script is needed.
  • Index cards, one per student
  • A board with two columns: Builds belonging and Breaks it
  • The take-home link to share afterward

Flow

  1. 3 minA place you belong: what makes it that way?
  2. 3 minDignity and respect, and the hard question
  3. 2 minBelonging versus fitting in
  4. 3 minWhat does fitting in cost? Turn and talk, share out
  5. 4 minSmall moments, builds or breaks, and the research
  6. 3 minTwo moments: the name, the plan
  7. 2 minWiden the circle, close

Short on time (10-minute check-in)

Dignity versus respect, belonging versus fitting in, small moments, and one way to widen the circle.

Before you teach
This is about everyone in the room, including you.

Dignity applies to the students who are hard to like, too. Model it in how you run the conversation: names said right, every answer taken seriously, no sarcasm.

Don't ask for stories of exclusion.

Being left out is painful, and retelling it in front of the people who did it can make it worse. Keep examples invented. Students can think of their own privately.

Dignity isn't agreement.

Some students will push back: "So I have to respect everyone?" Good question. The answer is the heart of the lesson: you don't have to respect what someone does, and you still treat them as a person with worth.

Watch for targeting in the room.

If a student laughs or looks at a classmate during the "breaks it" examples, the lesson may be landing on something real. Move on calmly, then check in privately and let a counselor know that day.

Name the adults' part too.

Belonging at school isn't only students' job. Adults set much of the culture. It's fine to say, "We're working on this too."

Where this comes from.

Floyd Cobb and John Krownapple's Belonging Through a Culture of Dignity argues that equity work rests on recognizing everyone's inherent worth. Donna Hicks's elements of dignity give the everyday moves on the student page.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Who already belongs?

Students who match the school's majority culture may not notice belonging, because they've always had it. Students of color, students new to the school, LGBTQ+ students, students with disabilities and students on financial aid often notice it every day.

Names.

Mispronouncing or shortening a name, especially a non-Anglo one, is one of the most common dignity hits in schools. Ask, practice, and get it right.

Money.

Inclusion often costs money at school: trips, gear, eating out, the right clothes. Students may be left out for reasons they can't fix. Keep examples free.

Faith and values.

Some students hold beliefs others disagree with, strongly. Dignity applies across those lines too. You can disagree with a belief and still treat a person with dignity.

Disability and neurodivergence.

Students who process social cues differently may be left out without anyone meaning harm. "Widen the circle" includes them.

Culture shapes how belonging looks.

In some families, belonging is about family and community first, and school belonging matters less. Respect that; the lesson is about how we treat people, not ranking where students belong.

What the research says

Cobb and Krownapple argue that belonging, built through a culture of dignity (the inherent worth of every person), is the foundation of equity work in schools, and that dignity differs from respect, which is earned.

Cobb & Krownapple, Belonging Through a Culture of Dignity, 2019

Hicks describes ten essential elements of dignity, including acceptance of identity, inclusion, fairness, benefit of the doubt and accountability, drawn from her work in international conflict resolution.

Hicks, Dignity, Yale University Press, 2011

First-year college students who spent about an hour learning that worries about belonging are common and fade with time showed lasting benefits: over three years, the intervention halved the achievement gap for Black students and improved their self-reported health.

Walton & Cohen, Science, 2011

A meta-analysis of 51 studies found that teacher support and students' own positive traits were the strongest predictors of school belonging.

Allen et al., Educational Psychology Review, 2018

The need to belong is a fundamental human motivation; lacking belonging is linked to a wide range of harms to health and well-being.

Baumeister & Leary, Psychological Bulletin, 1995
